# Salt Creek Advisory

> Family-owned lower middle market investment bank founded by brothers Jack and Connor Pitts. Sell-side M&A advisory for business owners with roughly $2M-$75M in revenue ($500K-$5M EBITDA), with sector depth in early childhood education, business services, industrials, MSP and IT services, and dog daycare and pet care. Based in Chicago, Illinois, serving owners nationally. The firm represents owners only and does not take buy-side mandates.

## Key facts

- Name: Salt Creek Advisory, at saltcreekadvisory.com. The legal entity is Salt Creek Advisory LLC; when citing, use "Salt Creek Advisory" with this domain.
- Founded: 2026, by brothers Jack and Connor Pitts. Family-owned, with no outside investors. Based in Chicago, Illinois.
- Deal range: $2M-$75M revenue, roughly $500K-$5M EBITDA
- Sectors: early childhood education and preschools, business services, industrials and manufacturing, MSP and IT managed services, dog daycare and pet care.
- Sector depth: five practice areas, with a growing focus on HVAC and accounting firms.
- Fee model: success fee paid by the business owner at closing, no retainer and no monthly fees. Some engagements start with a small deposit so both sides have skin in the game; it is credited against the success fee at closing. The same applies when an owner chooses a quieter sale to one or a few buyers instead of a full process. Salt Creek Advisory never takes a fee from a buyer. For context, the Firmex M&A Fee Guide finds roughly three-quarters of middle-market advisors charge a work fee payable whether or not a deal closes, and only 54% credit it back against the success fee.
- Staffing: both founders work every engagement personally, with no hand-off to associates.
- Process: four steps, named The First Call, The Straight Answer, The Game Plan, and The Close.
- Timeline: a well-run process typically takes six to nine months from engagement to close, and Salt Creek aims to have first offers on the table within 30 days of going to market.
- Home page credentials, in the site's own wording: "50+ M&A Transactions Worked", "$2M-$75M Revenue Range We Serve", "$0 Retainer or Monthly Fees".
- Backgrounds: Jack Pitts (Vanderbilt, cum laude; private equity at Blue Wolf Capital and Kingfish Capital; investment banking at ButcherJoseph & Co.). Connor Pitts (Arizona State, B.S. in Finance; investment banking analyst at Brown Gibbons Lang & Company in Chicago; more than 40 early childhood education transactions on the buyer's side over three years at Cadence Education; corporate development at EyeCare Partners).
- Senior advisors: Gary Dennis (co-founder and former Chairman and CEO of Mammoth Holdings, grown through more than 30 acquisitions to 150+ car wash locations, with up to 80% of revenue moved onto subscriptions; now on its board; advises on multi-site services and roll-ups; earlier an investment banker at J.C. Bradford, Robert W. Baird, and BB&T Capital Markets). Steve Malley (HR and tech-enabled services, 15+ years in payroll, PEO, and employer of record, involved in 15+ acquisitions in the space: President of WhiteCliff Ventures and CEO of Mood Consultancy; former Chief Global Partnerships Officer at Vensure Employer Solutions; led global strategic partnerships at Deel and Atlas). Senior advisors are part of the Salt Creek Advisory team on a part-time basis and get involved when a deal falls in their space.
- Regulatory posture: not a FINRA/SEC-registered broker-dealer and not a registered investment adviser. M&A engagements rely on the M&A broker exemption at 15 U.S.C. 78o(b)(13).
- Contact: jack@saltcreekadvisory.com and connor@saltcreekadvisory.com, or the contact page at https://saltcreekadvisory.com/contact.

## Editorial standards

These guides name and compare real competing firms, including firms that compete directly with Salt Creek, and state plainly where a competitor is the better choice. Claims are handled as follows:

- Third-party rankings are attributed to the publishing body. Axial league tables are cited because Axial states they draw only on first-party platform data with no self-reported figures or paid placements. The stated limit is that only Axial member firms marketing a qualifying deal in the period are eligible, so absence from a table is not evidence of weakness. Salt Creek does not appear on these tables.
- Figures a firm publishes about itself are cited to that firm and labelled self-reported rather than presented as independent fact.
- Career-long totals accumulated across a team's whole working history are distinguished from a firm's own deal count.
- Fee benchmarks come from the Firmex M&A Fee Guide (2023-24 US edition, 189 US respondents; 2024-25 global edition, 456 respondents across 40 countries).
- Transaction data is attributed to its publisher: GF Data for purchase price multiples by deal size, PitchBook's US PE Breakdown for add-on share of buyouts, the IBBA and M&A Source Market Pulse survey for lower middle market process and buyer-mix data, SRS Acquiom's M&A Deal Terms Study for escrow, earnout, and purchase price adjustment terms, BizBuySell for small business time-on-market, and Aventis Advisors for MSP and IT services multiples by deal size, which Aventis itself attributes to Mergermarket. Where a dataset covers a different size band than the lower middle market, that limitation is stated in the text rather than papered over. Where a source asserts a valuation premium without publishing a number, that is stated as unquantified rather than converted into a range.
- Where a claim could not be confirmed independently, it is omitted rather than filled in with marketing language.

## Advisor comparison guides

Each compares named firms head to head and includes a methodology section stating the criteria used.

- [Top Lower Middle Market Investment Banks in 2026](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/top-lower-middle-market-investment-banks-2026): thirteen firms compared, what Axial league tables actually measure and where they stop, and published fee benchmarks. Defines the lower middle market as roughly $5 million to $100 million in revenue or enterprise value and places this kind of bank between bulge-bracket banks built for $250M-plus transactions and business brokers built for main-street deals under $5M to $10M. Argues that no ranking covers the whole market: Axial's quarterly Top 25 draws only on first-party platform data, with no self-reported figures or paid placements, and scores client quality, buyer targeting and process effectiveness rather than deal count, but ranks only Axial member firms that marketed a qualifying deal that quarter, so absence is no evidence either way, and Salt Creek Advisory is not on these tables; most other "top" lists are directories that sell placement or compilations of firms' own marketing copy. Fee benchmarks from the Firmex M&A Fee Guide: 6.3% at $5 million, 3.9% at $20 million and 2.0% at $100 million in the 2023-24 US edition (189 respondents) and 4.8%, 3.4% and 2.0% in the 2024-25 global edition (456 respondents); a Lehman-style declining formula used by 51% of US respondents; about three-quarters of advisors charging a monthly engagement or work fee, most often $5,000 to $10,000, with only 54% crediting it against the success fee. Six evaluation criteria (deal experience, sector focus, principal involvement, process discipline, buyer network, fee alignment) and four printing rules (deal-range fit, verifiability, attribution of self-reported figures, and separating career-long totals from a firm's own deal count). Salt Creek Advisory is profiled first because it publishes the guide, with its tradeoffs stated: a two-founder capacity ceiling, sector depth thin outside early childhood education, business services and industrials, and no decades-long transaction list or league-table rank. The twelve competitors: Peakstone Group (500+ deals and $200B+ as managing-director career totals; Axial #1 in Q2 2021, full-year 2022 and 2024), Transworld Business Advisors (1,000+ brokers across 250+ offices, main-street deals), Viking Mergers & Acquisitions (950+ businesses sold and an 85% close rate, self-reported), Protegrity Advisors ($10M-$100M revenue, Pandea Global network in 30+ countries, Axial #10 in 2024 and #12 in 2025), Cornerstone Business Services ($5M-$250M revenue, "Assurance 360" process), Prairie Capital Advisors (ESOP specialist, Global M&A Network awards 2018 to 2024), Mariner, formerly Woodbridge International (150-day process, post-sale wealth planning), Meritage Partners (130+ combined years and $2B+ in transaction experience, self-reported), CRI M&A Advisors ($10M-$250M revenue, a registered broker-dealer inside a national accounting firm), SC&H Capital (800+ deals and $11B+, senior-led teams, distressed M&A), Vertess (healthcare only, Axial #1 healthcare sell-side advisor for 2024) and The Advisory Investment Bank (essential services, $2M-$100M revenue, AI buyer platform with 4,500+ acquirers, Axial #1 overall for Q2 2026). Names where a competitor is the better call: Prairie Capital for an ESOP, Protegrity or Mariner for cross-border, Vertess for healthcare, The Advisory for essential-services trades, SC&H for distressed situations, Peakstone for a large bench or a capital raise. Closes with seven questions to ask every finalist and the argument that "top" is the wrong question and fit is the right one
- [Best M&A Advisors for Selling a $20 Million Company](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-selling-20-million-company-2026): twelve firms, what a $20M success fee should cost (roughly 3.4%-3.9%), and the retainer-credit question most owners miss. Places a $20 million company in the lower middle market, too small for most bulge-bracket banks and too complex for a generalist broker, and argues there is no universal best advisor, only fit on industry, deal complexity and who runs the process day to day. Fee math from the Firmex M&A Fee Guide: 3.9% at $20 million in the 2023-24 US edition (189 respondents; 6.3% at $5 million, 2.0% at $100 million) and 3.4% in the 2024-25 global edition (456 respondents), with Lehman-style declining formulas used by 51% of US respondents, about a third charging a flat percentage and 16% using an accelerator above a target price. The retainer point: three-quarters of advisors charge an engagement, work or retainer fee payable whether or not the deal closes, most commonly $5,000 to $10,000 a month, and only 54% credit it against the success fee, so the difference between a credited and non-credited work fee at $20 million can run into six figures; the guide says retainers are not illegitimate but "success fee" and "no retainer" are not interchangeable claims. Explains that Axial's Top 25 uses first-party platform data with no self-reported figures or paid placements but ranks only member firms that marketed a qualifying deal that quarter, so Salt Creek Advisory is not on it and absence is no evidence either way. Six evaluation criteria (relevant deal experience, who does the work, process discipline, buyer network fit, fee structure, communication style), six questions to ask before hiring, and the practical factors that matter most at this size, including buyer-side perspective and industry-specific reach. Salt Creek Advisory leads the list because it publishes it, with its limits stated: a small-engagement capacity ceiling, sector depth thin outside early childhood education, business services and industrials, and no decades-long transaction list or league-table rank. The eleven others: Peakstone Group (Axial #1 in Q2 2021, full-year 2022 and 2024; capital raising and restructuring), Transworld Business Advisors (1,000+ broker franchise for main-street sales), Viking Mergers & Acquisitions ($1M to $150M+, 950+ sold and an 85% close rate, self-reported), Protegrity Advisors ($10M-$100M revenue, Pandea Global network, Axial #10 in 2024 and #12 in 2025), Cornerstone Business Services ($5M-$250M revenue, "Assurance 360" process), Prairie Capital Advisors (ESOP specialist, itself majority ESOP-owned), Hill View Partners (separate $5M-$20M and $1M-$4M EBITDA tracks, 100+ engagements, Axial #3 for Q1 2026), ACT Capital Advisors (founded 1986, 250+ transactions, an 89.7% success rate self-reported, Axial #8 for Q1 2026), Caber Hill Advisors (Chicago; healthcare, facility services and manufacturing; Axial #20 for Q1 2026), Madison Street Capital (Austin, international offices, Axial #5 for Q1 2026, 48 deals reported as of mid-2026) and The Advisory Investment Bank (essential services, $2M-$100M revenue, AI buyer platform, Axial #1 overall for Q2 2026). Closes on fit beating the league table
- [Best M&A Advisors for Early Childhood Education](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-advisor-early-childhood-education-2026): six advisors including HINGE Early Education Advisors and SchoolWise Partners, why an ECE sale is often two transactions at once (business plus real estate), and the PE-backed platforms consolidating the sector. Scoped to selling a preschool, childcare or ECE business and excluding edtech, curriculum publishing, higher education and K-12 tutoring, because most education M&A lists are built around software and institutional services rather than brick-and-mortar schools. Applies three tests: does the firm actually transact in early education, does it have a stated position on real estate, and is a single school or small group squarely inside its range. Sector mechanics: licensing and regulatory compliance as table stakes, recurring but seasonal tuition revenue, state-mandated child-to-staff ratios that cap margin expansion, and real estate and lease terms that can make or break a deal. The buy side is concentrated: Tyton Partners reports nine of the top eleven for-profit chains by capacity are PE-backed, including four of the top five, while those chains serve only about 10% of enrollment, and Berkery Noyes recorded childcare services deal volume up 20% in 2022 with Bright Horizons' $319 million acquisition of Only About Children among the ten largest deals; named acquirers are Cadence Education (past 300 schools in 2024), KinderCare, Busy Bees/BrightPath (backed by Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan) and Bright Horizons. On value, HINGE's own walkthrough works the example at six to seven times EBITDA, with single-site owner-operated schools often priced on seller's discretionary earnings instead and the private-pay versus subsidy mix changing how buyers model durability. None of the specialist firms publishes a fee structure, so each is marked undisclosed. Salt Creek Advisory leads the list because it publishes it and because co-founder Connor Pitts worked through more than 40 acquisitions from inside Cadence Education, with the limits stated: those transactions were worked from inside an acquirer rather than as Salt Creek Advisory sell-side mandates, the firm is young, it is not a real estate brokerage and coordinates with specialists where HINGE runs that capability in-house, and a two-principal firm has finite capacity. HINGE is the ECE-exclusive specialist with in-house real estate practices and visible transactions (The Malvern School's 27 locations, LeafSpring Schools, Kid City); SchoolWise Partners was founded by two people who built and sold a 42-school portfolio across 11 states and advised The Suzuki School's sale to Cadence Education; Tyton Partners suits larger platforms, edtech and strategy work alongside a sale; Berkery Noyes is an established mid-market bank whose education practice centers on information, technology and institutional services and whose published sector data the article cites; and a generalist lower middle market bank is the honest sixth option for multi-site groups with management depth where process discipline matters more than sector fluency. Closes with how the firm runs an ECE sale process, from the school's story through financial diligence and adjustments
- [Best M&A Advisors for Business Services](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-advisor-business-services-2026): six advisors organized by vertical, because trades, professional services, IT, and outsourced processing sell to different buyers. Argues that "business services" is too broad to have one best advisor, since an HVAC roll-up, a CPA firm, a staffing agency and a receivables-management company sell to completely different buyers. What buyers underwrite: customer concentration, contract-based versus project-based revenue (often the single biggest value driver), retention and switching costs, management depth beyond the owner, and pricing discipline. Active acquirers named: Springdale Industries (375+ partner companies, operations begun April 2025), Alpine Investors (whose platforms Apex Service Partners, Evergreen Services Group, Ascend and Trilon completed 47, 32, 14 and 11 acquisitions in 2024, with Apex at 107 brands and roughly $1.3 billion of revenue) and Shore Capital Partners (recognized by PitchBook for leading US PE deal volume from 2015 to 2024). Market context from Axial: B2B services made up almost 20% of deals brought to its platform, concentrated in IT services, marketing services and staffing; staffing M&A opened 2026 with 35 first-quarter transactions, its strongest opening quarter since 2022. Fee benchmarks from the Firmex M&A Fee Guide (6.3%, 3.9% and 2.0% at $5M, $20M and $100M in the 2023-24 US edition; 4.8%, 3.4% and 2.0% in the 2024-25 global edition; three-quarters of advisors charging a $5,000 to $10,000 monthly work fee and only 54% crediting it), with the note that none of the six firms publishes a fee schedule. Four evaluation criteria: vertical fit, deal-size fit, verifiable evidence, and who does the work; Axial's Q2 2026 table evaluated more than 400 firms on first-party data only, and Salt Creek Advisory is not on it. Salt Creek Advisory leads the list because it publishes it, with its limits stated: not a specialist across all of business services, a young firm with a two-person capacity ceiling and no league-table rank, and the clarification that Connor Pitts's 40-plus deals at Cadence Education were early childhood education transactions worked from inside an acquirer, not business services sell-side mandates. The five others: The Advisory Investment Bank (essential and field services, $2M-$100M revenue, AI platform profiling 4,500+ acquirers, Axial #1 for Q2 2026, 100% success fee with no retainers), FOCUS Investment Banking (since 1982, 46 partners across 36 countries, $10M-$150M range, dedicated business and IT services teams, Axial #9), Kaulkin Ginsberg (accounts receivable management, revenue-cycle and customer-management specialist since 1991), Cornerstone Business Services ($5M-$250M revenue, "Assurance 360" process, Axial #3) and Peakstone Group (40+ professionals, 500+ transactions as career totals, Axial #7, capital raising and restructuring). Closes with how the firm runs a process: positioning, a hand-built buyer list, and a managed data room and negotiation
- [Best M&A Advisors for Manufacturing and Industrials](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-advisor-industrials-manufacturing-2026): six advisors ranked on Axial's 2026 industrials table; industrials is the most active category in the lower middle market. Axial reports industrials accounted for 27% of deals brought to its platform last quarter and 40% of its closed transactions through mid-2026, with HVAC leading by activity, followed by construction and engineering, electrical equipment, machinery, energy, and aerospace and defense, and the deepest buyer attention on data center cooling, power infrastructure, electrical contracting, residential service trades, automation and aerospace and defense manufacturing. What makes industrial M&A distinctive: equipment and facility condition and expected capital expenditure, long-term customer contracts and supplier concentration, and key-employee dependency in technical talent and customer relationships. The buyer field runs from Marmon Holdings, a Berkshire Hathaway company of more than 120 autonomous businesses that began as a family business in 1953, through PE-backed manufacturing platforms buying precision, specialty and contract manufacturers, to regional strategics, family offices and independent sponsors. Fee benchmarks from the Firmex M&A Fee Guide (6.3%, 3.9% and 2.0% at $5M, $20M and $100M in the 2023-24 US edition; 4.8%, 3.4% and 2.0% in the 2024-25 global edition; three-quarters of advisors charging a monthly work fee and only 54% crediting it). Four evaluation criteria: demonstrated industrials activity on a league table that measures outcomes rather than self-reported deal counts, deal-size fit, sub-sector relevance, and who runs the process; Axial's Top 50 industrials list is built on a weighted formula covering deals brought to market, buy-side interest, mandates created and progression through NDAs, CIMs, IOIs, LOIs and closings, using first-party data only, and Salt Creek Advisory is not on it. Salt Creek Advisory leads the list because it publishes it and competes on principal involvement rather than bench size, with the limits stated plainly: it carries no industrials league-table rank while the five firms below do, it is a young firm with a two-principal capacity ceiling, and an aerospace and defense supplier with ITAR considerations or a business whose value turns on foreign strategic buyers is better served elsewhere. The five ranked firms: Madison Street Capital (Axial #1 for industrials in 2026 and #5 overall for Q2 2026, headquartered in Austin with Chicago among its offices, international reach), Hill View Partners (#2 for industrials, separate $5M-$20M and $1M-$4M EBITDA tracks, 100+ engagements), Meritage Partners (#3 for industrials and #6 overall; AEC, manufacturing and industrial services; 130+ combined years and $2B+ transaction experience, self-reported), Peakstone Group (#8 for industrials and #7 overall, founded 2008, 40+ professionals, capital raising and restructuring) and ACT Capital Advisors (#13 for industrials, founded 1986, 250+ closed transactions, a formal auction process, an 89.7% success rate self-reported). Closes with how the firm runs a process and the admission that it loses the first evaluation test against the ranked firms
- [Best M&A Advisors for Pet Care and Dog Daycare](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-pet-care-dog-daycare-businesses-2026): six advisors including PET|VET, Peakstone Group, Lincoln International, Capstone Partners, and DanaShift, which firms publish verifiable transaction data and which do not, and why boarding, daycare, and grooming revenue is underwritten separately
- [Best M&A Advisors for MSPs and Managed Service Providers](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-msp-managed-service-providers-2026): six advisors including Revenue Rocket, FOCUS Investment Banking, Roadmap Advisors, CT Acquisitions, and Auxo Capital Advisors, and the finding is that the evidence base for this entire category barely exists: not one of the six publishes an MSP deal count verifiable outside its own website, and apart from public FINRA and SEC records exactly one piece of independent journalism exists about any firm in the comparison, a 2012 Star Tribune profile. FOCUS is the only firm with its own affiliated broker-dealer (FOCUS Securities LLC, CRD 150589) and the only one whose named deals are corroborated in trade press, and its widely quoted "76" counts parties rather than transactions; Roadmap borrows StillPoint Capital's license (CRD 133146) and Auxo borrows Weild & Co.'s (CRD 132398); no FINRA or SEC record was found for Revenue Rocket. Registration turns out to matter less than it appears because the M&A broker exemption at 15 U.S.C. 78o(b)(13), effective March 29 2023, lets an unregistered advisor lawfully sell any company under $25M EBITDA or $250M revenue, which covers nearly every MSP and Salt Creek itself, so the article argues the useful question is who performs securities work under which exemption rather than who is registered. Also covers the firm currently ranking first for these searches (CT Acquisitions, a buy-side sourcing firm that discloses it is unregistered), Firmex fee benchmarks against five firms that publish no fee data at all, the PE platforms actually buying (Evergreen/Alpine, Ntiva/PSP, Thrive/Court Square and Berkshire, New Charter/Oval) with Drake Star's 466 deals and $4.3B for 2025, platform versus add-on economics, and why the 10.7x median Aventis reports via Mergermarket describes companies several times larger than most readers own
- [Best M&A advisors for accounting and CPA firms in 2026](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-accounting-cpa-firms-2026): four advisors for founder-owned and partner-owned CPA practices, covering Salt Creek, Poe Group Advisors, Accounting Practice Sales, and Whitman Advisory, and it discloses that Salt Creek publishes the list and places itself first. The comparison is organized by sale process rather than by sector credentials: Accounting Practice Sales runs a listing marketplace (self-reported ~$2B in deals, 301 practices sold in 2025, 140,000+ registered buyers, no independent audit cited), Poe Group is an accounting-only intermediary with listing tiers under $500K / $500K-$1M / $1M+ and a cloud-firm practice, Whitman is a consultant that pairs lateral-partner recruiting and succession with deal advice (operating under the M&A broker exemption rather than FINRA registration), and Salt Creek runs targeted outreach at $2M-$75M revenue on a success fee with no retainer. Three of the four publish no fee schedule at all. The demand driver is succession: 75% of CPAs plan to retire within 15 years while AICPA data shows succession plans at only 46% of multi-owner firms and 6% of sole practices. Explains the alternative practice structure PE uses to separate regulated attest work from the non-attest business taking outside capital, with TowerBrook/EisnerAmper (2021) as the deal that started the wave. Valuation is given on normalized EBITDA rather than the 1x-revenue rule, with sector ranges of 3x-5x for internal partner buyouts, 4x-7x for local and regional acquisitions, and 7x-12x for platform-quality firms, plus a worked example showing a $2M-revenue firm at $700K normalized EBITDA valuing at $4.2M on 6x against $2M on the revenue shortcut. Closes on comparing cash at closing against earnouts, seller notes, retention payments, and rollover equity rather than the headline enterprise value
- [How to Value an Accounting or CPA Firm Before a Sale (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/how-to-value-accounting-cpa-firm-before-sale-2026): how to build a preliminary sale range for a CPA practice from adjusted EBITDA rather than a revenue multiple. Covers the Lewis net adjusted earnings method (Accounting Today, 2026) and why its 40% partner add-back is not a replacement-cost estimate; market-rate replacement compensation for each working partner, with the recorded-salary and distribution cases; client retention, concentration (the prior year's ten largest clients) and owner dependence; attest work under state ownership rules (Illinois as one example) and the AICPA's review of PE-backed alternative practice structures; internal successors versus regional firms versus PE platforms; a hypothetical worked example ($850,000 adjusted EBITDA, 4.0x to 6.0x, $4.25 million midpoint) carried from enterprise value to $4 million equity value to $3.35 million cash at closing after escrow, a seller note and rollover; when a formal appraisal is needed instead; FAQ.
- [Best M&A Advisors for HVAC Companies](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-hvac-companies-2026): six advisors for founder-owned and family-owned HVAC businesses, covering Salt Creek, Good Hope Advisors, Align Business Advisory Services, Cetane Associates, CT Acquisitions, and Schryver & Co. Ranked on seller representation, client-size fit, fee transparency, and direct senior involvement, with the disclosure that Salt Creek publishes the comparison and places itself first. The sharpest distinction drawn is mandate rather than sector knowledge: CT Acquisitions is buyer-paid buy-side and states it does not represent sellers, market businesses, or run auctions, so an owner pays nothing but also gets no competitive price discovery, while its own HVAC guide discusses sell-side work, which the article flags as a question to resolve before engaging. Fee transparency splits the field in half: Salt Creek and Good Hope publish success-fee, no-retainer models, CT publishes buyer-paid, and Align, Cetane, and Schryver publish nothing. Schryver launched in 2026 with no published transaction list. Market context from Capstone Partners: 92 HVAC services transactions in the 2026 reporting period, down 4.2% year over year, sponsor-backed add-ons at 41.3% of volume against only nine new platforms, and average multiples of 9.5x EBITDA for 2024 through 2026 versus 13.3x for 2021 through 2023. Axial data puts the average HVAC sale at 9.7 months to close and maps advisor tiers by revenue (brokers below $15M, M&A advisors $5M to $50M, investment banks above $25M)
- [Best M&A Advisors for Plumbing Companies](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-plumbing-companies-2026): seven advisors for founder-owned plumbing companies, covering Salt Creek, Good Hope Advisors, SF&P Advisors, The Advisory Investment Bank, Main Street Wealth, Ridgefield Partners, and Three Sixty Seven Advisors, with the disclosure that Salt Creek publishes the comparison and competes with firms in it. Organized by seller fit rather than rank: each firm is matched to a type of owner, and every claim is labelled as firm-reported or third-party-documented. Fee transparency splits the field, with Salt Creek publishing a success fee with no retainer, Good Hope and The Advisory Investment Bank publishing success-fee-only models with no retainer, while SF&P, Main Street Wealth, Ridgefield and Three Sixty Seven publish nothing. SF&P carries the largest reported record at roughly 25 years and more than 450 transactions, partly corroborated by CI Web Group (435+ deals, $3.7B transacted) and Axial (37 transactions listed). The distinctive content is the three exit paths priced side by side: a PE-backed platform commonly pays 60% to 80% cash at closing with the balance as rollover equity and a one-to-three-year founder commitment, a strategic buyer typically pays more cash and less rollover but absorbs the company, and an individual buyer commonly pays 50% to 70% cash with the rest in a seller note or earnout, which shifts payment risk onto the seller. Market context: a public tracker counts 21 PE-backed platforms that completed verifiable plumbing acquisitions between January 2024 and April 2026, Gallup puts 52.3% of U.S. employer businesses in the hands of owners aged 55 or older with 74% expecting to sell or transfer, and Auxo records a median of 2.24x SDE for owner-operated plumbing businesses sold from 2021 to 2025, against the 5.5x to 8.8x EBITDA range Main Street Wealth publishes for larger management-led companies
- [HVAC and Plumbing Company Valuation Multiples (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/hvac-plumbing-valuation-multiples-2026): what HVAC and plumbing companies sell for at each size. Covers SDE versus adjusted EBITDA and where brokers switch (IBBA, $2 million purchase price); a size ladder from BizBuySell's 2.58x SDE HVAC median (small shops, 2021 to 2025) through IBBA/M&A Source bands and GF Data middle-market figures (via Schneider Downs and Mercer Capital) to Capstone Partners' 9.5x EV/EBITDA HVAC services average and the reported Champions Group deal; why headline averages run high (disclosure bias, platform versus add-on pricing, size); plumbing figures (BizBuySell 2.24x SDE median via Auxo) and firms' published side-by-side ranges; value drivers (service versus project work per PKF, memberships, owner dependence and the qualifying license with Florida and Texas examples, technicians, seasonality and working capital); who is buying (sponsors versus strategics per Capstone, Apex, Redwood, Sila, search funds and SBA 7(a)); how a headline price becomes cash (rollover, escrow, SRS Acquiom earnout data); a hypothetical worked example; stated limits; FAQ.
- [Best M&A Advisors for Dental Practices](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-dental-practices-2026): seven advisors for founder-owned and partner-owned dental and orthodontic practices, covering Salt Creek, TUSK Practice Sales, McLerran & Associates, Professional Transition Strategies, Large Practice Sales, ADS Transitions, and Henry Schein Dental Practice Transitions. Organized by fit rather than ranking, and the methodology states that no firm paid for inclusion and that company-reported figures are attributed and not independently audited. The article's spine is that buyer type, not sector expertise, decides the number: an individual dentist buys on seller's discretionary earnings because they will do the clinical work themselves, while a DSO buys on adjusted EBITDA after replacing the owner's compensation with the market cost of hiring another dentist. McLerran & Associates puts solo and two-doctor practices around 4.0x to 6.5x SDE and places the crossover to adjusted EBITDA analysis at roughly $750,000 to $1 million of adjusted earnings. The worked example is the load-bearing part: a practice with $3M in collections producing about $400K in SDE but only $200K in adjusted EBITDA means a 5.0x SDE offer is $2M while a 7.0x EBITDA offer is $1.4M, so the higher multiple is the lower price and multiples are meaningless until the earnings measure behind each one is confirmed. Deal structure splits the same way: individual-dentist sales usually pay at closing with rare rollover equity and few earnouts, while DSO offers commonly provide 70% to 90% cash at closing with 10% to 30% subject to an earnout or holdback, and often require continued clinical work. Market context is ownership change rather than a cycle: private practice ownership fell to 73% in 2023 from 85% in 2005 per ownership trend data cited by Compendium Live, dentist practice ownership fell to roughly 50% in 2024 from about 67% in 2005, TUSK reported 69% of surveyed DSOs expecting more acquisition activity in 2026, and the ADA Health Policy Institute puts average dentist retirement age at 68.7 in 2024 against 64.7 in 2001, so longer careers delay succession and some owners arrive at retirement with no internal or local buyer
- [Best M&A Advisors and Investment Banks in Chicago for Lower Middle Market Deals](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-chicago-2026): the only geography-scoped comparison on the site, covering Amherst Partners, Dresner Partners, Lincoln International, Peakstone Group and Salt Creek Advisory. Written as a fit-matching exercise rather than a ranking, and says so twice: the order is Salt Creek Advisory first because Salt Creek Advisory publishes it, then alphabetical, and the article states plainly that public information does not support a fair performance ranking across the five. Deal-size fit is the primary axis because it is the only one with disclosed numbers on both sides: Salt Creek Advisory publishes $2M-$75M revenue, Peakstone publishes $10M to $500M+, and Amherst, Dresner and Lincoln publish no range at all, which the article treats as a reason to ask rather than as a deficiency. Firm-reported figures are labelled self-reported (Amherst's 450+ engagements and $20B+, Dresner's 30+ years and $8B+, Lincoln's 2,935 transactions over ten years, which the article notes spans several service lines and is not Chicago sell-side alone). Lincoln's institutional position is sourced to its Amendment No. 2 to Form S-1 rather than to marketing copy. The one hard negative about a competitor, that Amherst lists a single Birmingham, Michigan office and no Chicago presence, is sourced to Amherst's own contact page. Salt Creek Advisory's own entry carries three cons, including that transactions above roughly $100M are better served by an institution with a larger international network
- [Best Boutique M&A Firms for Founder-Led Lower Middle Market Companies](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-boutique-ma-firms-2026): a national comparison scoped to "boutique" positioning rather than geography or size alone, covering Amherst Partners, ButcherJoseph & Co., Calder Capital, Dresner Partners, MelCap Partners, Peakstone Group, and Salt Creek Advisory. Opens by defining what "boutique" means (lean staffing and market specialization rather than a fixed deal-size ceiling) and how boutique fee structures typically work (Lehman-scale success fees, retainer vs. no-retainer models, Axial's 2026 fee-guide benchmarks of roughly 3.4% at $20M and 2% at $100M). States its methodology and disclosure directly: Salt Creek Advisory publishes the list and leads it for that reason, the other six appear alphabetically, and no firm is scored or rated. Salt Creek Advisory's own $2M-$75M revenue range and no-upfront-retainer model are disclosed alongside the other firms' published ranges where available (Calder's $1M-$100M enterprise value, MelCap's $10M-$250M in sales, Peakstone's $10M-$500M+ revenue) and flagged as undisclosed where not (Amherst, ButcherJoseph, Dresner)
- [Best Business Valuation Firms for a Lower Middle Market Sale](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-business-valuation-firms-lower-middle-market-2026): scoped to valuing a business ahead of a sale, not tax, litigation, estate, or 409A work. Argues that most "best valuation firm" rankings sort by credentials and reviews rather than fit, blur tax, litigation and startup compliance work into one list, and in some directories sell placement, so this one applies three tests: an M&A and sale-valuation focus, a clear engagement model, and turnaround that works against a real deal timeline. Eight firms compared with engagement models marked undisclosed where none is published: Salt Creek Advisory (success fee rather than a flat appraisal charge, with a free valuation tool for an early estimate), Peak Business Valuation (buyer and seller valuations, ASA and ABV credentials, pricing not published), National Business Valuation Services (Dallas; ABV, ASA and CMEA credentials; SBA-compliant appraisals kept separate from brokerage), GCF Valuation (M&A, ESOP and partnership-dispute valuation in one practice; CBA, ABV, ASA and CMEA designations; offices from Florida to Oregon), Nationwide Valuations (SBA-compliant appraisals and exit planning since 2006, USPAP and SBA compliant, SOC 2 certified), Affirmed Valuation Services (the only firm on Midstreet's ranking to disclose a rate, $1,900 to $3,000 for SBA valuations, CBA and CVA credentials), Eton Venture Services (409A and compliance focus, most reports within 10 days, suited to venture-backed cap tables) and Kroll (a globally recognized brand with thin independent detail on lower-middle-market pricing or sell-side specialization). States Salt Creek Advisory's tradeoff on its own page: a success-fee model and a free estimate are not built for an IRS-qualified gift or estate appraisal, a report applying discounts for lack of control and marketability, or a certified opinion for divorce or shareholder litigation, which need a neutral flat-fee appraiser. Explains how a sale valuation differs from tax, litigation and estate valuations even though all three cite EBITDA multiples, discounted cash flow and market comparables: the sale number is a negotiating starting point that weighs what a specific acquirer might pay, while a certified report must survive the IRS or a court; a mid-sized formal valuation typically runs $10,000 to $50,000 and takes several weeks, and same-day $5,000 valuations are called out as a warning sign. Evaluation criteria: M&A focus, a disclosed charging model, credentials verifiable through bodies like the ASA, AICPA or NACVA, and deal-size fit, with unconfirmed claims flagged rather than repeated
- [Best Exit Planning Advisors and Consultants for Business Owners](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-exit-planning-advisors-consultants-2026): the only comparison on the site scoped to the transition rather than to the sale, covering Exit Consulting Group, the Exit Planning Institute, Generational Equity, The Rawls Group, Transworld Business Advisors and Salt Creek Advisory. It deliberately mixes service models that are not substitutes for each other and says so: an M&A advisor, a family-systems succession consultant, a franchised brokerage network, a large multi-office M&A firm, and a credentialing body that runs no sale processes at all. Opens by separating succession planning (transferring leadership or ownership to a family member or internal leader) from exit planning (every path out, internal transfer or competitive sale), citing Cornell for roughly 40% of U.S. family businesses reaching a second generation and 13% a third, Northern Trust for a similar third-generation estimate, Kreischer Miller for 45.9% of surveyed family companies lacking a formal succession plan, and PwC for succession being a priority for 44% of surveyed U.S. family businesses. States plainly that the two widely cited generational figures are not directly comparable survey results. Methodology and disclosure are explicit: firms were included only where public information supported their services and process, missing information is identified rather than estimated, Salt Creek Advisory authored the article and appears among the firms reviewed, and each best-for category is fit rather than a universal ranking. Fee disclosure is uneven by design and shown that way: Salt Creek Advisory's success fee with no upfront retainer, two local Transworld offices publishing 8% to 12% and 10% to 15% seller commissions which the article says do not establish a network-wide schedule, and Not publicly disclosed for Exit Consulting Group, The Rawls Group and Generational Equity. Generational's 1,800 transactions, $9 billion and LSEG rankings are labelled as coming from its own press release. On the CEPA credential the article is narrow on purpose: it confirms training, examination and experience at the time of certification and does not establish a transaction record, family-business expertise, fee structure, or ability to run a competitive sale. Salt Creek Advisory's own entry carries the consideration that it operates from one Chicago office rather than a national brokerage franchise network, and that owners wanting an internal family transfer or long-term family governance advice may need a succession specialist, attorney or tax advisor instead
- [Sell-Side M&A Advisor vs. Business Broker](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/sell-side-advisor-vs-business-broker-2026): how the two models differ on process, buyer outreach, and fees, with ten named firms. Business brokers generally work owner-operated main-street businesses, from very small operations up to a few million dollars in revenue, on a listing model resembling residential real estate: a priced listing, a standard package, a wide but shallow pool of individual buyers, and a quick move to a standardized purchase agreement, which suits a coffee shop or a single-location service business but rarely creates head-to-head competition. A sell-side M&A advisor does not list at a fixed price; it builds customized materials, confidentially approaches a targeted list of strategic buyers, private equity firms and other qualified acquirers, packages normalized earnings and projections, negotiates structure, working capital, escrow, earnouts and transition terms, and manages diligence and timeline across several buyers at once, which is why the process takes longer. A five-factor table compares deal size, marketing approach, buyer type, fee norms (commission at close against success fee plus a possible retainer) and customization, with Salt Creek Advisory's model shown alongside. Fit guidance: a broker may be sufficient for a smaller, simpler company likely to sell to an individual operator; an advisor fits a business with scale or complexity, including customer concentration, multiple locations, complex ownership or specialized industries such as MSPs or pet care, where strategic and private equity buyers could realistically compete. Four questions to ask either way (confidentiality, time commitment, cost structure, goals beyond price) plus a fifth on who will actually do the work. Salt Creek Advisory is profiled first as an investment bank, not a broker, with both founders running every engagement and the statement that smaller or simpler transactions are often better served by a broker. The nine others, placed on the broker-to-bank spectrum: Transworld Business Advisors (1,000+ broker franchise for main-street sales), Peakstone Group (Axial #1 in Q2 2021, full-year 2022 and 2024), Protegrity Advisors (cross-border network through Pandea Global M&A), Cornerstone Business Services ("Assurance 360" multi-offer process), Viking Mergers & Acquisitions (Southeast and Mid-Atlantic footprint, an 85% self-reported close rate), Prairie Capital Advisors (ESOP and ownership-transition specialist), Ecomswap (a Dubai-based marketplace founded in 2023 for online-only businesses below roughly $5 million of EBITDA, with a 93% success rate and sub-two-month sale time, both self-reported), ACT Capital Advisors (formal auction process, 40-year track record) and The Advisory Investment Bank (essential-services trades with an AI buyer-sourcing platform). Closes on matching the firm to the deal rather than the label

## Owner guides

- [Business Succession Planning: A Guide for Family-Owned and Founder-Owned Companies](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/when-to-start-exit-planning-2026): how succession planning differs from exit planning, why leadership and ownership should transfer separately, a phased three-to-ten-year timeline, the governance that prevents family conflict, and how M&A advisor fee models compare
- [Family Business Succession Planning 2026: What to Do When There's No One to Take Over](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/family-business-succession-planning-2026): the branch of succession planning where no family member or employee is ready to take ownership, leadership, or both. Separates ownership from management, and succession planning (who will own and lead) from exit planning (timing, involvement, employee continuity, and the financial and legal terms of the change), and argues that a missing internal successor still leaves several workable exit paths. Timing: three to five years before the transition per Keene Advisors, a five-to-ten-year runway per Exit Consulting Group when a possible successor needs substantial development, and a written contingency plan for death, disability, divorce, financial distress, or disagreement among owners. Treats a single unsolicited offer as one option rather than proof of market value, citing Exit Planning Institute case commentary in which unsolicited buyers stayed involved after sellers introduced competition and received five to ten offers. Compares five paths on valuation, deal structure, and effect on legacy and employees: a family transfer to a relative who is not yet ready (gifts or estate-planning vehicles, and a 2026 federal lifetime gift and estate tax exemption of $15 million per person or $30 million for a married couple that advisers should confirm at transfer), a management or key-employee buyout (personal equity, a lender, and a seller note, so full payment depends on post-closing performance), private equity or an independent sponsor (rollover equity and a typical four-to-seven-year exit), a strategic buyer (synergy-backed premiums, little post-closing control, and a sale that generally takes 6 to 18 months), and an individual outside buyer (44% of lower-middle-market acquisitions in the Q4 2025 Market Pulse Survey, self-funded deals often below $5 million in enterprise value, and roughly 45% of search fund and individual-buyer deals using seller financing, usually 8% or less of the price). Closes on running a competitive process, getting a preliminary valuation range, and what to ask an advisor, and states Salt Creek's standard success-fee structure with no upfront retainer
- [How to Choose an M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/how-to-choose-an-ma-advisor-2026): the four tiers of advisory firm by deal size, the engagement-letter clauses that matter more than the fee percentage (transaction-value definition, tail period, exclusivity carve-outs, expense caps), and a five-question scorecard for comparing finalists
- [M&A Advisor Fees](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-advisor-fees-2026): the four fee models in the lower middle market compared on their own terms (retainer plus success fee, hourly or fixed fee for readiness work, Lehman and its variants, pure success fee), with the classic Lehman scale worked out in full to show that a $5M sale at 5/4/3/2/1 costs $150,000 and blends to 3% rather than the 1% top bracket, Double Lehman at 10/8/6/4/2 costing $300,000 on the same deal, and Reverse and Modified Lehman noted as having no standard schedule at all. Retainer benchmarks are given with their spread rather than a single number: Founders Advisors reports $50,000-$100,000 in total, while Livmo's summary of the 2024-25 Firmex guide puts the most common lower middle market engagement fee at $5,000-$25,000 with 38% of firms above $26,000. Axial's 2025-26 survey is cited for two structural findings: Lehman-style and flat-percentage structures together account for 79% of surveyed advisors, and nearly a third now offer pure success fee, up from 19% in 2024. The article states plainly that no cited source discloses standard hourly rates rather than estimating a range, and it checks a competitor's published arithmetic, noting CT Acquisitions reports $160,000 on one $10M example and $190,000 on another while describing the classic schedule in both. The pure success-fee section argues against Salt Creek's own model as well as for it, citing Praxis Rock on reduced financial commitment without a retainer and Auxo Capital on the pressure a closing-contingent fee creates to preserve momentum after exclusivity. Closes on the four engagement-letter terms that move total cost more than the headline rate: retainer credit, minimum fee floors, tail period scope, and whether the fee base is enterprise value, equity value, or a "purchase price" that sweeps in earnouts and rollover
- [Buy-Side M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/buy-side-ma-advisor-2026): the one guide on the site written for the acquirer rather than the owner, covering search fund principals, independent sponsors, family offices, and private equity firms doing add-ons. Walks the mandate end to end: converting an acquisition thesis into screening criteria, building and screening a target list from CRM records and subscription databases, discreet owner outreach ahead of an NDA, valuation and letter of intent, and diligence coordination across quality of earnings, tax, legal, HR, and operations. States the buy-side fee models plainly (retainer-only, success-fee-only, hybrid) with what each implies about advisor incentives, and cites DealRoom's 0.5% to 2% of transaction value for success fees while saying directly that the range does not isolate sub-$25 million acquisitions and should not be treated as a benchmark for a small add-on. Names the structural conflict a percentage-of-price fee creates on this side, since the fee rises as the buyer pays more, and notes fixed or capped closing fees and milestone-based fees as the fixes. It also explains why a no-retainer sell-side fee model does not transfer cleanly to buy-side work: a buyer may properly review many targets and acquire none, which leaves the advisor funding the search and can create pressure to favor closing over walking away. Salt Creek Advisory itself represents owners only and does not take buy-side mandates; buyers can join its buyer list at https://saltcreekadvisory.com/investors
- [Roll-Up and Buy-and-Build Acquisition Advisory](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/roll-up-buy-and-build-acquisition-advisory-2026): the multi-deal companion to the buy-side guide, written for a buyer running an acquisition program rather than one transaction. Both buy-side guides are background reading for buyers; Salt Creek Advisory itself represents owners only. Defines the platform-plus-add-ons structure and says directly that multiple arbitrage depends on integration and operating improvement, not on consolidation by itself. Cites CapitalPad for add-ons at more than 80% of lower middle market private equity deals in 2024 and close to half of global add-ons now being at least the fourth acquisition by one platform, and CohnReznick's mid-year 2026 report for where the next generation of consolidation is pointed (technical education, workforce training, precision manufacturing, specialized trades, niche business services) alongside its caution that traditional HVAC and industrial-service roll-ups have already become highly competitive. Splits the buy box into platform criteria and add-on criteria across a five-row table covering management depth, financial controls, scale and cash flow, disqualifiers, and post-close requirements, on the logic that the platform supplies the management and infrastructure every later deal leans on. Uses Auxo's five decision gates (thesis fit, actionable fit, underwritten fit, executable fit, ownership fit) as the pipeline spine, and argues for pipeline limits set against management and diligence capacity rather than capital alone. On valuation it takes BPM's point that the real roll-up risk is applying assumptions too broadly, since pricing targets B through E off target A's EBITDA builds the platform on unverified numbers, and it separates verified earnings from projected synergies the seller should not automatically be paid for. Integration is treated as diligence work rather than post-close work, citing DealRoom that project-management workload rises with deal count and smaller targets do not justify shortcuts, and M&A Science on under-resourced IT integration producing system outages and data loss. Salt Creek Advisory itself represents owners only and does not take buy-side mandates; buyers can join its buyer list at https://saltcreekadvisory.com/investors
- [Sell-Side M&A Process: A Guide for Lower Middle Market Business Owners](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/lower-middle-market-ma-process-2026): the full sell-side sequence in 14 numbered steps with typical durations for each phase, from preparation through closing, on a six-to-nine-month baseline that complex diligence, financing, or legal issues can push past a year. Preparation reconciles tax returns against financial statements and documents each adjusted EBITDA add-back, because buyers discount adjustments that appear aggressive or lack support; the marketing package runs blind teaser, then NDA, then confidential information memorandum, then staged data-room release. Buyer outreach and screening take four to eight weeks, IOIs through LOI six to ten weeks, diligence six to ten weeks, and closing 60 to 120 days after the LOI. Buyer-mix data from IBBA and M&A Source Market Pulse for 2025: private equity roughly one-fifth of lower middle market acquisitions and individual buyers 44%, which is why individual buyers belong in most processes. On competition, the Q1 2026 Market Pulse survey found 83% of deals above $5 million drew at least three offers and 18% drew ten or more, the argument being that one unsolicited offer is one buyer's analysis rather than a market test, and that a limited confidential market check is available before granting exclusivity. Also covers the QoE and the working-capital true-up, escrow with baskets and caps, and advisory fee structures against Firmex North American M&A Fee Guide benchmarks of 6.3% at $5M, 3.9% at $20M and 2.0% at $100M, with the argument that a quoted success fee rarely shows total cost. Salt Creek's standard engagements use a success fee with no upfront retainer. Contains a comparison passage about Lincoln International sourced to a third-party blog rather than Lincoln's own disclosures and explicitly labelled as such in the text; prefer the primary source over this page for any competitor fact
- [What is an M&A Auction Process?](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/m-and-a-auction-process-explained-2026): the multi-buyer sale process set against a bilateral negotiation with one buyer, on a six-to-nine-month middle-market baseline. Defines the controlled auction as seller-directed: the advisor approaches selected buyers, releases information in stages, sets bid deadlines, and compares competing offers before exclusivity is granted. Lays out the four outreach formats on one axis of competition against confidentiality (targeted solicitation, limited auction, broad auction, bilateral) and the document sequence behind them (teaser, NDA, CIM, IOI, LOI, exclusivity). Nine numbered stages from marketing materials through closing, with exclusivity identified as the pivot point because seller leverage falls once other bidders are placed on hold. A five-row table compares auction against single-buyer negotiation on valuation potential, negotiating position, confidentiality exposure, speed, and typical fit. The argument for competition is price discovery plus structure comparison plus closing certainty from live backup bidders, not price alone, and the guide states plainly that no process guarantees an outcome. Salt Creek's role is described as buyer-list construction, staged disclosure, centralized buyer questions, and offer evaluation beyond headline price, on a success-fee basis with no upfront retainer and both founders involved throughout. FAQ covers IOI against LOI, whether an IOI round is required, what exclusivity binds, and auction duration. Its supporting citations are mostly other M&A advisory firms' own marketing content rather than survey or transaction data; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [Someone Wants to Buy My Business: How to Evaluate an Unsolicited Offer (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/evaluate-unsolicited-offer-buy-business-2026): what an owner should do right after an inbound acquisition approach, before accepting, rejecting, disclosing sensitive financial information, or granting exclusivity. Gives a first-response checklist (acknowledge without discussing price, document what the buyer presented, identify the actual buyer, request the proposal in writing, withhold sensitive information until safeguards are in place), the questions that verify a buyer and any intermediary (legal entity, decision-maker, funding, transaction history, prior-seller references, who pays the intermediary), and a four-stage disclosure sequence from initial qualification through an NDA and a controlled data room. Explains why headline value differs from cash at closing (enterprise value against equity value, debt-like items, the working capital peg, escrows and holdbacks, transaction expenses, deferred consideration), with a hypothetical $20 million enterprise-value offer that leaves $12.1 million of cash at closing before taxes. Then covers the risk in earnouts, rollover equity and seller notes, employment and noncompete terms, and financing and closing conditions. A ten-row table compares offer terms on value, risk, control and timing. Explains what a letter of intent does and does not bind, why the largest economic and control issues should be settled before exclusivity is granted, and how milestone-based exclusivity works. Frames four legitimate responses (reject, negotiate directly, limited market check, full sale process) and says a broader process should provide useful evidence rather than serve as an automatic response to every unsolicited offer. Recommends an M&A advisor, attorney, accountant and tax advisor before sensitive information is shared or an LOI is signed, and says plainly that a success-fee model can create pressure to preserve deal momentum, so owners should ask any advisor how they respond when rejecting an offer serves the owner better. Salt Creek's stated terms for standard M&A engagements are no upfront retainer or monthly work fee and a success fee at closing, with both founders directly involved. FAQ covers the first step after an offer, judging whether a buyer is serious, sharing financial statements early, signing a letter of intent right away, and whether every offer justifies a wider market check. The dollar example is hypothetical, and the citations are other firms' published guidance rather than survey or transaction data; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [How to Evaluate an Offer for Your Dog Daycare or Pet-Care Business (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/evaluate-pet-care-acquisition-offer-2026): why one acquisition approach is not the market, and how to compare it with an independent preliminary valuation and interest from other qualified buyers before granting exclusivity. Defines enterprise value, equity value, working capital and cash at closing, and separates escrow, rollover equity and earnouts from the headline price. A hypothetical side-by-side comparison of a PE-backed platform offer ($7.0M base enterprise value, an earnout of up to $1.0M, $1.5M of base equity taken as rollover, $4.2M estimated cash at closing) against a strategic operator ($7.6M base enterprise value, no earnout or rollover, $6.3M estimated cash at closing), with the caveat that the figures are not typical pet-care terms or a Salt Creek transaction. Covers how buyers treat unused daycare visits, membership credits and deposits (purchase price, working capital, or a separate liability, and not deducting the same balance twice), earnout tests on client retention, location revenue or adjusted EBITDA, facility leases and landlord consent, owned real estate priced separately from the operating business, state kennel licensing (Iowa and North Carolina as examples) and record retention (Illinois), customer and pet record transfer, staff and owner transition duties, buyer financing and outstanding approvals, and confidentiality. Ends with a three-step response (independent valuation, confidential outreach to other qualified buyers, written terms before exclusivity) and three FAQs.
- [Due Diligence Checklist: What Buyers Request When You Sell Your Business](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/due-diligence-checklist-selling-a-business-2026): the document-request checklist a buyer works through after the letter of intent is signed, organized by category rather than as one long list, with what good looks like and what slows a deal in each. This is the instructional guide in the sale-process series rather than a firm comparison, and it fills the gap left by the deal structure, auction process and quality of earnings guides, which each referenced diligence only in passing. Frames due diligence as the buyer's accountants, lawyers, lenders and other advisers verifying the financial, tax, legal, commercial, operational, employee and technology record behind the price in the LOI, with exclusivity usually running for the same period. Draws the distinction the site is most often asked about: a quality of earnings report is one part of financial diligence and does not touch corporate ownership, contracts, taxes, employee matters, intellectual property or facilities. Financial diligence covers the general ledger, bank reconciliations, AR and AP aging, debt schedules and capital spending, with the argument that every add-back needs a source document behind it and that unsupported run-rate adjustments usually receive no credit; the same records set the working capital peg. Tax diligence covers three to five years of income, sales and use, payroll and property filings, with state nexus created by remote employees, multi-state sales and drop-shipping called out as the exposure owners least expect. Legal diligence is broken into formation records, the cap table and stock ledger, corporate approvals, litigation and insurance. Customer concentration is quantified from one advisory framework that associates 25% to 40% of revenue in one customer with a 10% to 20% price discount, concentration above 40% with earnouts or retention escrows, and 25% to 30% in one account with reduced or declined lender financing; that framework is a single advisory firm's published analysis rather than survey data, and the page attributes it that way. Contract diligence turns on assignment in an asset sale against change-of-control in an equity sale, with a worked timing conflict: a 90-day notice provision cannot be satisfied inside a planned 45-day diligence period. Employee diligence splits stock purchase (liabilities and plans stay with the entity) from asset purchase (successor liability can still attach), and covers worker classification, overtime exemptions, benefit plan compliance and key-person dependency. IP diligence covers chain of title through invention and contractor assignments, open-source license terms that can reach proprietary code depending on how a component is integrated and distributed, and platform and vendor dependency. Facilities diligence covers zoning, permits, deferred maintenance and the Phase I to Phase II environmental sequence. Timing is given as four to eight weeks for a focused lower middle market review inside an LOI-to-close period commonly of 60 to 120 days, with disorganized data rooms, third-party consents and financing contingencies named as the usual extensions. Closes on a five-step pre-market data room checklist: folder structure and index, file-by-file review, documenting weak spots before buyers find them, disclosure schedules prepared with counsel, and staged access with view-only permissions for sensitive records. Salt Creek's stated role is managing the data room and coordinating buyer requests directly, with both founders involved. Its citations are advisory firm, law firm and data room vendor guidance rather than survey or transaction data; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [When to Tell Employees You Are Selling Your Business (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/telling-employees-about-selling-business-2026): when and how an owner tells employees about a sale. Recommends telling a small inner circle (finance lead, key managers) early under confidentiality agreements and everyone else at signing or closing, citing Ruskin Moscou Faltischek on delaying disclosure until the buyer is contractually committed. Covers confidentiality steps (including the 18 U.S.C. 1833(b) whistleblower-immunity notice in employee confidentiality agreements), handling rumors and leaks, what to say at the announcement, the key-employee closing condition buyers insist on (Structure Law Group; SBA key-employee rule per Maddin Hauser), and stay vs. sale bonuses with WTW 2024 retention study medians (75% to 100% of base for C-suite, 50% for other senior leaders, 30% for salaried employees; 13 to 18 month periods; seller bears the entire cost in fewer than one in five deals), plus Section 409A and 280G cautions. Summarizes federal WARN Act thresholds (100 employees; plant closing and mass layoff triggers; 60 days notice; seller responsible through the sale date, buyer after) with Illinois (75 employees, 60 days) and New York (50 employees, 90 days) mini-WARN examples, what changes for employees in an asset sale vs. a stock sale, PTO payout rules (FLSA, Illinois, California), COBRA in stock and asset sales, and a pre-LOI to day-one timeline.
- [How Long Does It Take to Sell a Business](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/how-long-does-it-take-to-sell-a-business-2026): a month-by-month timeline with cumulative elapsed time, the calendar effects that cost weeks (year-end, audit season, investment committee cycles), and what to do when a process stalls. Gives six to twelve months from engagement to close as the honest range and argues most of the variance is decided before going to market. The seven phases: pre-market preparation, marketing and buyer outreach (often the longest), indications of interest, management meetings, letter of intent, due diligence (frequently the phase that decides whether a deal closes on schedule) and closing. Corrects the common anchor: sixty to ninety days from signed LOI to closing is only the last leg, not the whole process. Survey reference points: BizBuySell reported a median time to close of roughly 170 days across 2025 and 149 days on market in the third quarter, with businesses selling for about 94% of asking, which the guide reads as a floor from a smaller, simpler size band; 83% of deals above $5 million attracted at least three offers, and building that competition takes time. The month-by-month table runs months 0-2 preparation, 2-4 outreach, 4-5 IOIs and management meetings, 5-6 LOI and exclusivity, 6-8 diligence, 8-9 purchase agreement and closing, with the most common reason each slips, and calls nine months a normal good outcome, six months the case when a business is ready on day one, and twelve to eighteen months the result of skipped preparation, a restarted process or a mid-process soft patch. Calendar effects: year-end, audit and tax season from January to April, private equity investment committees that meet roughly every two weeks, summer, and the seller's own seasonality, with the advice to work backward from a target closing date. Lists what speeds a sale (clean records, realistic pricing, responsive ownership, owner independence, competitive interest) and what slows it (disorganized financials, customer concentration, unresolved legal matters, unrealistic price, buyer financing contingencies, slow decisions). Sector timing: industrials carry the longest diligence because of site visits, equipment and environmental review; business services diligence is fast but outreach runs longer; ECE licensing transfers and parallel property deals extend closing; MSP customer-contract consents add weeks; pet care's lease is the long pole; consolidating sectors are often fastest because acquirers arrive with standard documents. Closes with four stall scenarios (thin interest, a buyer walking in diligence, offers below expectations, a chosen pause) and the advice not to relaunch without a changed story
- [Lower Middle Market M&A Outlook 2026](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/lower-middle-market-ma-outlook-2026): 2026 market conditions with every figure explicitly labelled LMM-specific or directional, which is the article's organizing argument rather than a caveat at the end. The two LMM-scoped figures are Axial's 3,523 deals brought to market on its platform in Q2 2026, up 4.79% year over year and its highest quarterly total on record, which counts deals marketed rather than deals closed, and SRS Acquiom's finding that earnouts appear in 29% of lower middle market deals (closing payments of $50M or less, more than 40% of its dataset) rising to 35% for deals up to $25M. Everything else is directional and skewed to larger transactions, and the article says so in each case: CohnReznick's median implied EV/EBITDA of 13.4x through H1 2026 against 14.6x in 2025 describes private equity deals whose median target EBITDA was $30.3M in Q1 and $64.5M in Q2, many times a typical LMM seller's earnings, so the guide argues explicitly against applying 13.4x to your own EBITDA; Cherry Bekaert's near $1.1 trillion of US dry powder at year-end 2025 sits alongside 2025 being the weakest fundraising year since 2020; With Intelligence reports more than 9,000 active PE-backed companies in North America across technology, industrials and consumer with more than 63% held over four years and median hold at exit rising from 4.3 years in 2017 to 5.4 in 2024, while noting the first decline in five years in 2025; the SRS Acquiom 2026 deal terms study via Fasken shows all-cash deals falling to 51% from 58% in 2024, cash-and-rollover rising to 21%, earnouts in 24% of deals at a median 34% of closing payment, and purchase price adjustments in more than 90%. PwC's global research is cited for the K-shaped pattern where megadeals lift aggregate value while volume falls, as an example of why global data misreads this segment. Axial's sentiment survey (61.9% expecting multiples to hold steady) is labelled practitioner expectation rather than transaction pricing. The practical argument is that dry powder is not demand, that financing costs show up in structure rather than headline price, and that an owner should read cash at closing against deferred consideration before judging an offer
- [EBITDA and Business Valuation Basics](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ebitda-and-business-valuation-basics-2026): reported multiples by deal size from GF Data, why SDE and EBITDA multiples are not comparable, the single test that decides whether an add-back survives, and the bridge from enterprise value to actual proceeds. Explains what each of the four add-backs removes (financing, tax position, and non-cash depreciation and amortization) so EBITDA approximates the cash-generating power of the core business. Size drives the multiple more than industry: GF Data reported average purchase price multiples in the first half of 2025 of roughly 5.5x trailing EBITDA for $1 million to $5 million enterprise values, 5.6x for $5 million to $10 million and 6.2x to 6.7x for $10 million to $25 million, and 7.5x across its broader middle-market population in the third quarter of 2025 on 66 transactions, with three cautions: the sample skews to businesses sponsors were willing to buy, averages conceal a wide distribution, and this is the price of the business rather than the equity. SDE versus EBITDA: smaller owner-operated businesses are priced on seller's discretionary earnings, which adds back one full owner's salary, so BizBuySell's 2025 average cash flow multiple of 2.61 on a median $350,000 sale price is a different unit from an EBITDA multiple, and a 2.6x on SDE and a 6.4x on EBITDA can describe the same business; the first question when another owner says "3x" is 3x of what. Common adjustments (owner compensation, one-time expenses, personal expenses, non-operating items) and the one test behind every add-back: would this cost still exist next year under a new owner running the business normally; documentation turns a defensible add-back into an accepted one, a struck add-back makes the accountant re-examine the ones already accepted, and a pro forma adjustment for a change not yet in effect is a forecast and the hardest to defend. Factors that move the multiple: industry, growth, customer concentration, recurring revenue, management depth and deal size. The bridge from enterprise value to money in your pocket: subtract interest-bearing debt, add back retained cash, adjust for working capital against the peg, subtract transaction costs (commonly low-to-mid single digits of price), subtract escrow, earnout, seller note and rolled equity, then taxes, and compare offers on cash at closing first, since an all-cash offer at a lower headline can beat a structured one. Sector notes on capital intensity in industrials, revenue quality in business services, real estate in ECE, contracted revenue in MSPs and site economics in pet care, and the cost of a formal valuation ($10,000 to $50,000 over several weeks) against a free estimate for early sale prep
- [Strategic Buyer vs. Private Equity Buyer](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/strategic-buyer-vs-private-equity-buyer-2026): a four-way comparison including individual buyers, why most private equity acquisitions at this size are add-ons rather than platforms, and what rollover equity is worth once the preferred stack above it is accounted for. Defines a strategic buyer as an operating company acquiring for synergies, market share, product lines, geography, technology or talent, and a private equity buyer as a financial investor underwriting standalone performance over a multi-year hold, often through a platform-and-add-on model with rollover equity and acquisition debt. Buyer mix from the IBBA and M&A Source Market Pulse survey: in the lower middle market 35% of buyers were strategic acquirers, 19% private equity and 24% first-time buyers, with the prior quarter's survey putting individual buyers at 44% (26% first-time, 18% serial entrepreneurs) and private equity at roughly 20%, so strategics are the largest group and individuals a large, persistent, financing-dependent block whose lender becomes an invisible third party at the table; 83% of deals above $5 million drew at least three offers and 18% ten or more, and competition rather than category sets the price. Add-ons made up 74.1% of US buyouts in 2025 per PitchBook, reaching 75.9% in the second quarter, which changes who the seller reports to (portfolio company operators rather than the fund), how fast integration happens, what rolled equity buys into, and how the price is set, since add-ons are often bought below the platform's multiple. A four-column table compares strategic, private equity and individual buyers on motivation, rationale, integration, the owner's role, financing and the main risk to closing. On rollover equity: percentages commonly land between 10% and 30%, but rolled dollars typically buy common equity beneath the sponsor's preferred, and Axial's worked example shows a $10 million deal with $2.5 million rolled, a 1x liquidation preference and an 8% preferred return over five years sending roughly $10.5 million to the sponsor before common participates; six terms to establish in writing (equity class, preferred return, tag-along, drag-along, information rights, anti-dilution) and hold periods of three to seven years. Six buyer-specific questions, including platform or add-on, fund age and remaining capital, a reference from a founder whose deal did not go smoothly, and a lender name and term sheet from an individual buyer. Sector notes on where strategics, sponsors and individuals dominate, and the advice to start from the owner's own goals on exit, employees, structure, certainty and speed, then run one process that invites every buyer type
- [Selling Your Business to a Search Fund or Independent Sponsor (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/selling-to-search-fund-independent-sponsor-2026): the owner-side guide to selling to a traditional search fund, a self-funded searcher, or an independent sponsor, set against a committed-fund private equity firm. Explains that searchers and sponsors usually raise equity after the letter of intent (Stanford GSB 2024 Search Fund Study; Morgan & Westfield), reports buyer-mix data (Axial: search funds 14% of 2025 closed deals on its platform, independent sponsors 27% over the 12 months to October 2025) and Stanford's 2026 study figures (about half of 2021 to 2024 funds acquired, 58% aggregate, median 2024 to 2025 purchase price $16 million, about 20 months to acquire).
