Covers financing (investor equity, senior and junior debt, seller notes, SBA 7(a) up to $5 million), the SBA SOP 50 10 8.1 rules effective October 1, 2026 (full-standby seller notes as equity, limited sources capped at half the 10% injection, earnouts prohibited, 100% purchase with no seller stock or employment, consultant up to 24 months, lender valuation and QoE at $3 million), closing risk and exclusivity (Axial Dead Deal Report), typical asks (seller note, earnout, rollover, transition while the searcher becomes CEO), sponsor fees (McGuireWoods survey), a seven-question vetting list, pros and cons against strategic and private equity buyers, and a comparison table.
- [What Buyers Look for in an Acquisition Target](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/what-buyers-look-for-in-an-acquisition-target-2026): the customer-concentration thresholds buyers actually apply, what a quality of earnings review tests, how the working capital peg moves proceeds, and how unresolved risk converts into escrow and earnout terms. Frames the five factors buyers measure every target against: financial performance and quality of earnings, growth trajectory and market position, customer and revenue concentration, owner dependency and management depth, and operational and legal cleanliness, with the argument that buyers are pricing risk and every unresolved risk returns as a lower number or a worse structure. A quality of earnings review is not an audit: it runs four tests (add-back substantiation, revenue recognition and cutoff, run-rate versus trailing performance, working capital normalization), a round-number add-back with no paper trail gets struck, and a sell-side review commissioned before going to market finds problems at the owner's own pace rather than in week six of exclusivity. The working capital peg: nearly every deal is cash-free, debt-free with a normalized target usually averaged over the trailing twelve months, deliver less and the price falls dollar for dollar, aggressive pre-closing collections can lower the seller's own peg, and SRS Acquiom's study of more than 2,200 private-target deals closed 2019 to 2024 found more than three-quarters used a special-purpose escrow for the purchase price adjustment, so the peg calculation belongs in the LOI. Concentration thresholds: 10% is where a customer becomes a disclosed fact under US accounting standards, above roughly 20% most buyers treat it as material and adjust, above roughly 30% the response becomes an earnout, a larger holdback or contract reassignment before closing, and lenders underwrite concentration more conservatively than buyers, with three qualifiers (contracted multi-year revenue with assignment provisions, concentration that is an industry characteristic, and relationships held by management rather than the departing owner). Owner dependency is the one flaw that costs with every buyer type at once. Market Pulse data: 83% of deals above $5 million attracted at least three offers and 18% ten or more, and the buyer field was 35% strategic, 19% private equity and 24% first-time buyers, each stress-testing a different weakness. A translation table shows how each buyer worry becomes a term: earnouts for sustainability doubts, retention holdbacks for a key customer, transition periods and deferred payment for owner dependence, indemnity escrow for undisclosed liabilities, a true-up escrow for a light balance sheet; SRS Acquiom data puts earnout payouts at roughly 21 cents on the dollar outside life sciences, 68% of earnouts on more than one metric, and the median general indemnification escrow at 10% of transaction value without representation and warranty insurance against 0.5% with it, so "$18 million with $4 million in earnout" should not be compared to $16 million all-cash as though it were $18 million. Sector notes on what each buyer pool interrogates hardest, and the advice to start preparation years ahead and address concentration before going to market
- [How to Make Your Business Less Dependent on You (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/reduce-owner-dependence-before-selling-2026): how an owner reduces owner dependence (key-person risk) before selling. Defines the three-month test (how the business would perform if the owner could not work for three months, per Value Builder), reports Value Builder's owner-dependent vs owner-independent offer multiples (about 2.9x vs 3.9x earnings, owner-reported), shows how dependence moves deal terms (earnouts, holdbacks, longer transitions, SBA SOP 50 10 8.1 limits of a 24-month seller consultancy and no seller earnouts), and gives seven steps: a second layer of management with written authority, moving customer relationships to account leads, owner out of sole selling, documented processes, shared control of money and systems, stay bonuses (WTW 2024 medians) and key-person insurance, and practice absences. Covers why buyers already deduct a market-rate replacement for the owner in adjusted EBITDA, a 36-month timeline, options for owners selling within a year, and a checklist.

- [How to Prepare an MSP for Sale: A 24-Month Readiness Checklist (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/msp-sale-readiness-checklist-2026): a sale-preparation timeline for managed IT services owners, ordered by what takes longest to change, with C4 Solutions' recommended 12- to 24-month preparation period as the frame. At 24 months: separate true managed-services monthly recurring revenue from recurring invoices that lack a signed agreement, move break-fix clients to managed-service agreements at renewal (CT Acquisitions estimates recurring, contracted revenue can command an EBITDA multiple 1.5 to 2 times the multiple applied to project revenue, presented as an illustration rather than a standard premium), account for the weighted-average remaining contract term, and build a management layer so sales, escalations, and key client relationships no longer depend on the founder (Founder M&A lists lower offers, longer earnouts, larger escrows, and multi-year employment requirements as buyer responses). At 12 months: review assignment and change-of-control clauses, which can require customer consent even in a stock sale, and reduce customer concentration, treating a single client above 20 to 25 percent of revenue as worth watching and 5 to 10 percent per client as a cleaner profile, as screening benchmarks rather than a pass-or-fail test. At 6 months: reconcile financial statements to the general ledger and tax returns, reconcile PSA records with financial reporting, enforce ticketing discipline, confirm RMM endpoint counts match invoices and contract seat counts, and document SLA performance, which Auxo Capital identifies as evidence buyers examine in MSP diligence. Explains how unresolved issues move into deal structure (earnout, escrow, seller note, rollover equity) when there is less than 24 months to prepare, and closes with a seven-question self-check

- [Dental Practice Valuation Multiples (2026): What DSOs and Private Buyers Actually Pay](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/dental-practice-valuation-multiples-2026): how dental practices are priced by earnings measure and buyer type. Solo, owner-operated practices under roughly $500,000 in earnings are usually valued on seller's discretionary earnings (SDE), while associate-driven and multi-location groups are valued on adjusted EBITDA after deducting market-rate compensation to replace the owner's clinical and management work; CT Acquisitions places the common transition at roughly $750,000 to $1 million of adjusted annual earnings, though owner dependence and staffing can matter more than the threshold. Reported ranges for Q2 2026 come from CT Acquisitions, a secondary aggregator citing named industry sources whose original reports were not verified: 4.0x to 6.0x SDE under $500K, 4.5x to 6.5x SDE at $500K to $1.0M, 6.5x to 9.0x adjusted EBITDA at $1.0M to $3.0M, 8.0x to 11.0x at $3.0M to $10.0M, and 10.0x to 15.0x at $10.0M or more. Scott Leune's commentary is a separate, imperfect cross-check at 4x to 6x for smaller single locations, 7x to 10x for two or three locations and 9x to 12x for four or more, and neither source provides transaction-level data confirming the 12x to 15x range. McLerran & Associates' worked example ($1.5 million revenue, $600,000 net cash flow, $300,000 EBITDA) values one practice at $1.3 million to an individual dentist and $2 million to a DSO; private-buyer sales typically pay 100% cash at closing, DSO offers often 60% to 70% cash plus equity or an earnout, so a $2 million offer with 65% at closing pays $1.3 million up front. Per Dental Transitions, range position improves when the owner generates less than 60% to 70% of revenue, hygiene exceeds 30% of collections and private pay is at least 60% of revenue, and suffers when the owner produces more than 90% of doctor production or the lease has fewer than five years remaining. CT Acquisitions estimates a 1.0x to 3.0x EBITDA premium for orthodontic and oral surgery practices, which Auxo Capital Advisors, Peony and 1st Source Bank decline to quantify. DSOs grew from roughly 100 in 2010 to more than 2,000 by 2023 per a Georgia Dental Association summary, and Duckett Ladd reports DSOs courting practices valued at roughly $500,000 to $5 million in suburban and midsized markets.

- [EBITDA Add-Backs: A Seller's Guide to What Holds Up (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ebitda-add-backs-2026): a seller's working manual for adjusted EBITDA. Defines add-backs and the two-part test (the cost will not continue under new ownership, and a document proves the amount); covers SBA SOP 50 10 8.1 (effective October 1, 2026), which requires a lender-commissioned quality of earnings report documenting every add-back for initial acquisitions and business expansions priced at $3 million or more excluding owner-occupied real estate, and makes unjustified adjustments ineligible; a table of common add-backs with the proof each needs (owner pay above market, personal and family expenses, one-time costs, deal costs, related-party rent, discretionary giving); removal of PPP, ERC, EIDL and other non-recurring income; add-backs buyers reject (recurring 'one-time' costs, the SEC two-year test, run-rate and projected savings, lost revenue); negative adjustments (underpaid owner, below-market rent, unfilled positions, deferred maintenance, cash-to-accrual); the tax question of adding back personal expenses (IRC 162 and 262, IRS Publication 535, the 20% accuracy penalty); consequences when add-backs fail (Axial Dead Deal Report 21.3%, Express Scripts v. - [How to Prepare a Dog Daycare Business for Sale in 2026](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/prepare-dog-daycare-business-for-sale-2026): a two-phase sale-readiness timeline for dog daycare, boarding, and pet resort owners, split between the work that needs 12 to 24 months of documented operating history and the records confirmed in the final three to six months, with a workstream table covering financials, staffing, customer records, leases and licenses, safety documentation, and facility. On earnings: why buyers recalculate adjusted EBITDA from tax returns and the general ledger, why an owner-compensation add-back has to be netted against the market cost of replacing the owner's duties, why related-party rent needs comparable leases or an appraisal, and why buyers may reduce or reject adjustments that lack transaction-level support. On owner dependence: delegation has to be provable from scheduling and incident records rather than an org chart, and continued dependence tends to surface as a longer transition or an earnout. On staffing: the IRS common-law test and the Labor Department's separate economic-reality test can classify a groomer as an employee despite a Form 1099, and Form I-9s must be retained for three years after hire or one year after separation, whichever is later. On memberships: a $425 unlimited plan is about $35 per visit at 12 visits a month and about $24 at 18, churn is the share of renewal-eligible plans that did not renew (25 of 250 is 10%), and unreconciled prepaid packages may be treated as a liability rather than recurring revenue. On lease and licensing: a change of ownership is often a deemed assignment requiring landlord consent, an estoppel certificate fixes the lease facts, Iowa animal welfare licenses are expressly non-transferable and require a new application and inspection, and North Carolina uses a change-of-ownership form instead, with both states given as illustrations rather than nationwide rules. Also covers incident and insurance files, including the care, custody, and control exclusion that can leave an injured animal uncovered under a standard general liability policy, and facility condition, including the Facility Condition Index ($150,000 of deferred maintenance against a $3 million replacement value is 5%) as a screening tool rather than a valuation rule
- [How to Prepare a Preschool or Childcare Business for Sale in 2026](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/prepare-preschool-childcare-business-for-sale-2026): a two-phase sale-readiness guide for preschool, childcare and daycare owners, split between the structural work that needs 12 to 24 months of documented operating history and the diligence records assembled in the final three to six months, with an eight-row timeline table mapping each workstream to its transaction effect. On enrollment: a waitlist is not proof a center can add children, buyers compute occupancy classroom by classroom rather than center-wide, reducing licensed capacity for closed rooms, staffing limits, facility restrictions and schedule conflicts to reach usable capacity, then separate full-time-equivalent and paid enrollment from names on an attendance sheet; in a 2024 NAEYC survey 56% of directors reported under-enrollment against available slots, driven by staffing shortages, compensation and affordability. On revenue: private-pay and subsidy revenue are tested separately because billing terms and collection timing differ, four records (rosters, attendance, billing, cash receipts) are reconciled monthly by classroom, prepaid tuition is generally a deferred revenue or contract liability until the care is delivered and may be treated as debt-like rather than working capital in a deal, and CACFP receivables need their own reconciliation. Families pay about 68% of childcare costs in the United States, and personnel commonly runs 50% to 60% of a provider's expenses, so state child-to-staff ratios decide whether added enrollment converts to margin. On staffing: Cleveland Fed research found roughly one-third of surveyed centers at 20% or more annual turnover while 44% reported none, so a center's own staffing record carries more weight than a sector average, and an owner-compensation add-back has to be netted against a market-rate replacement salary. On credentials: CCDF background checks before employment and at least every five years, plus fingerprint, sex-offender and child-abuse registry searches, with an expired credential able to take a classroom out of usable capacity even when the licensed seats remain. On licensing and real estate: inspection, complaint and incident files organized by location with proof of remediation, lease assignment, change-of-control and landlord recapture rights, zoning and certificates of occupancy as a separate layer from state licensing, normalized market rent when the owner holds the building, an ASTM E2018 property condition assessment and CPSC playground guidance for deferred maintenance. On closing: licensing approval often sets the practical closing date, with Kentucky (a license cannot be sold or transferred), Georgia (Pre-K funding, Quality Rated status, CAPS and CACFP each approved separately), Texas (a qualifying ownership change revokes the permit; an expedited process was published March 6, 2026) and California (CACFP notice 60 days before the sale, buyer application 45 days before) given as illustrations rather than nationwide rules. Closes with a six-category preparation checklist covering enrollment and capacity, financials, staffing, licensing, real estate and insurance
- [Manufacturing Valuation Multiples](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/manufacturing-valuation-multiples-2026): why the two figures everyone quotes for manufacturing are both wrong: GF Data publishes no public sector breakout at all (7.5x in Q3 2025 and 7.2x full-year, all-industry, private-equity-sponsored, $10M to $500M enterprise value), and the widely repeated Capstone figure of 11.1x rising does not appear in Capstone's Annual Industrials M&A Report, which shows industrials at 8.9x in 2025 down from 9.3x in 2024 against a 2018-2025 average of 10.2x and a 2022 peak of 11.4x, so the claim inverts the actual direction of travel; the defensible read is roughly 7.2x where only sponsors bid against 8.9x where strategics were 52.4% of deal flow, plus the cash EBITDA calculation subtracting three-year average maintenance capital expenditure, and what certifications like AS9100 and ISO 13485 actually gate access to
- [The Working Capital Peg in M&A](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/working-capital-peg-ma-2026): how the post-closing purchase price adjustment works, the SRS Acquiom finding that working capital adjustments now appear in more than 90% of private-target deals against 50% a decade ago, that buyers' proposed calculations are reviewed and ultimately accepted in 7 of every 10 purchase price adjustments (not 7 of 10 disputes, which is a common misstatement of that study), and six specific traps with arithmetic: unmodeled seasonality, reserve methodology shifts, deferred revenue, cash-free debt-free definitions, and double-counted commissions
- [Business Services Valuation Multiples](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/business-services-valuation-multiples-2026): why the 7.4x composite everyone quotes for business services has no traceable public source (GF Data's own releases and ACG's carry no sector breakout, and the two published sub-sector ladders contradict each other on the same verticals without disclosing sample sizes), and why the distinction that actually drives the spread is that contracted revenue is not recurring revenue, evidenced from audited SEC filings rather than assertion: Rollins discloses roughly 75% recurring revenue with multi-year relationships and Cintas over 95% of revenue from route servicing, while Robert Half tells shareholders clients can terminate on short notice without penalty, ABM's agreements are cancelable on 30 to 90 days' notice and re-bid on renewal, and EMCOR warns its signed backlog may not result in actual revenues
- [M&A Deal Structure: The Six Ways Buyers Build an Offer](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-deal-structure-2026): why two offers at the same headline valuation can deliver very different proceeds, and the six components buyers assemble an offer from: cash at closing (and why an all-cash offer still carries holdbacks, escrow, and post-closing adjustments), earnouts (median around 31% of closing payments over roughly 24 months outside life sciences per SRS Acquiom via the Harvard Law School Forum, with the choice of metric and the definition of milestones as the two fight-starters), rollover equity (commonly 10% to 30% in middle-market deals, where the equity class matters more than the percentage: Axial's model shows a 25% rollover returning $6.25M on a $25M second exit as common equity but roughly $3.6M once a 1x liquidation preference plus an 8% preferred return sits ahead of it), seller notes (usually 10% to 30% of price at 6% to 8% over three to seven years, with subordination and SBA standby as the underweighted risk, since a note can be current under its own terms and still unpayable when the senior lender blocks payment), working capital adjustments, and staged or multi-step deals using put and call options over two to five years with the second tranche priced off future EBITDA
- [Earnouts, Escrows, and Holdbacks](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/earnouts-escrow-holdbacks-2026): why the headline purchase price does not show how much payment risk a seller retains, and the distinction between the two mechanisms most often confused with each other: an earnout pays only if the business reaches agreed performance targets after closing, while escrow and holdback reserve part of an already agreed price against defined indemnification claims and do not depend on future performance at all. Covers the revenue versus EBITDA choice (revenue shields the seller from post-closing expense and overhead decisions but still needs definitions for recognition, refunds, customer credits, and sales to other buyer-owned companies; adjusted EBITDA gives the buyer a profitability measure but leaves the P&L under buyer control, so staffing, marketing, and corporate overhead allocations can lower it while sales hold steady), escrow mechanics (a neutral third-party agent holds the funds, whereas a holdback leaves the money with the buyer and adds buyer credit risk, which is why sellers generally prefer escrow; Versailles Group guidance cites roughly 10% to 20% of purchase price over 12 to 24 months, with the explicit caveat that specific terms can fall outside those ranges, and representations and warranties insurance reduces but does not eliminate the reserve because policies often exclude known issues), non-financial triggers including customer retention and product or regulatory milestones, when an earnout is likely to appear (recent growth exceeding the pace supported by historical results, founder-led companies with less developed reporting, and sponsor-backed buyers, where the seller must identify which legal entity actually owes the payment since an acquisition subsidiary or portfolio company may owe it rather than the fund), and five dispute vectors a seller can negotiate against before signing: imprecise metric definitions, accounting judgment, information access without review rights, buyer operating decisions such as diverting sales to another subsidiary, and the independent-accountant process that keeps an accounting disagreement out of litigation. Sources are the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance (A&O Shearman), Kroll, Versailles Group, Auxo Capital Advisors, and Davis Wright Tremaine. The practical argument is that an earnout is risk retained after the sale rather than cash already earned, so a lower all-cash offer can be worth more than a higher headline number tied to a metric the buyer controls
- [How Sellers Protect Themselves After Closing](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/seller-risk-protection-deal-structuring-2026): the four mechanisms that decide how much of an agreed purchase price a seller actually keeps, and why they are one negotiation rather than four. Escrow places part of the price with a third-party agent (a holdback leaves it with the buyer and adds buyer credit risk); SRS Acquiom data puts the median general indemnification escrow at 10% of transaction value without representations and warranties insurance against 0.5% with it, on holding periods commonly of 12 to 24 months. An indemnification cap limits total recoverable losses, and ABA Private Target Deal Points Study data summarized by Morse shows 86% of deals capping below the purchase price, almost 40% between 1% and 10%, and most R&W-insured deals below 1%. A basket sets the threshold a claim must cross, and the distinction that costs real money is deductible against tipping: with a $1M threshold and $1.5M of losses a deductible basket costs the seller $500,000 and a tipping basket can cost the full $1.5M; 67% of baskets are deductibles, most are 1% or less of transaction value and 56% are 0.5% or less, and every R&W-insured deal in the study used a deductible. A survival period sets the claim deadline, with 90% of deals at 18 months or less for non-fundamental reps, fundamental reps often running three to six years or indefinitely, and tax reps tracking the statute of limitations. The headline cap is not the maximum exposure, because carve-outs sit outside it: fraud in 90% of deals, due organization 74%, due authority 73%. Buy-side R&W insurance moves covered unknown breaches to an insurer, priced at roughly 3% of the coverage amount (and falling, with sub-3% no longer uncommon) on limits of about 10% of transaction value and a retention of about 0.5% to 1%, plus a $25,000 to $50,000 underwriting fee and often a $100,000 to $150,000 minimum premium, which is what makes it proportionally expensive on smaller deals. It is not a shield against fraud, and it excludes known and diligenced issues, covenant breaches, forward-looking promises, and purchase-price and working-capital adjustments, so a separate escrow often survives alongside the policy. Sources are SRS Acquiom, the ABA study via Morse and Hirschler, Versailles Group, Koley Jessen, Linden Law Partners, Policyholder Pulse, and Fasken. Includes ten questions to put to an advisor and deal counsel before signing
- [Asset Sale vs. Stock Sale: What Business Owners Need to Know in 2026](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/asset-sale-vs-stock-sale-2026): how the two legal forms of a business sale differ for the seller. An asset sale transfers specified assets and the liabilities the buyer expressly assumes, while the seller keeps the entity, subject to successor-liability exceptions (de facto merger, mere continuation, fraudulent transfer, and environmental and state tax rules); a stock sale transfers ownership of the entity, which keeps its known and unknown liabilities, and an LLC sells membership interests instead. A nine-row table compares what is sold, liabilities, contracts and leases, employees, licenses and permits, seller tax character, buyer asset basis, closing complexity and typical preference. A hypothetical company ($20 million revenue, $3 million adjusted EBITDA, 60 employees, one leased facility, one major customer contract, a pending $300,000 warranty claim) runs through every section. Covers assignment and change-of-control consents for contracts, leases and licenses; employee continuity, accrued paid time off, COBRA, WARN and W-2 reporting; tax treatment by entity type, the seven-class residual method on Form 8594 with an illustrative $10 million allocation, and Section 338(g), 338(h)(10) and F reorganization structures; state successor tax liability and bulk-sale clearance; how diligence and closing documents differ by structure; statutory mergers; and how indemnification, baskets, caps, escrows and representations and warranties insurance allocate risk within either structure. FAQ covers whether an LLC sale is a stock sale, whether a buyer can require an asset sale, whether employees keep their jobs in a stock sale, whether a stock sale always lowers the seller's taxes, and what a Section 338(h)(10) election does. All figures are illustrative, the page states it is general information rather than legal or tax advice, and its citations are IRS and Department of Labor guidance plus law, accounting and advisory firm publications rather than survey or transaction data; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [What You Keep After Selling Your Business (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/what-you-keep-after-selling-a-business-2026): how a headline enterprise value becomes the cash an owner keeps. Ten items in three groups: what comes out at closing (debt and debt-like items, the working capital adjustment against the peg, transaction expenses with Firmex 2023-24 US fee figures of 6.3% at $5 million, 3.9% at $20 million and 2.0% at $100 million); what gets paid later or never (indemnification escrow, median 10% without and 0.5% with representation and warranty insurance per SRS Acquiom 2026; earnouts in 29% of lower middle market deals and paying about 21 cents on the dollar outside life sciences; seller notes and rollover equity); and what taxes take (2026 federal capital gains thresholds from IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32, ordinary income on Section 1245 recapture, inventory and noncompetes, purchase price allocation under Section 1060 and Form 8594, the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax and the material participation exception, C corporation double tax and Section 1374, and state rates for Texas, Florida, Illinois, Washington and California). A hypothetical $20 million offer falls to $12.1 million of cash at closing before taxes, and an Illinois owner at top rates pays roughly $250,000 to $288,000 per $1 million of long-term capital gain. Planning moves cover allocation, personal goodwill, Section 453A on large installment notes, Section 1202 qualified small business stock under both the pre- and post-July 4, 2025 rules, and the $15 million 2026 estate and gift exclusion. All figures are illustrative, the page states it is general information rather than legal or tax advice, and its citations are the Internal Revenue Code, IRS publications, state tax authorities and SRS Acquiom deal data; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [Letter of Intent: What to Negotiate Before You Sign (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/letter-of-intent-selling-a-business-2026): what a seller should do with a letter of intent before signing it. Explains which provisions usually bind on signing (exclusivity, confidentiality, expenses, governing law, per Mintz) and how promises to negotiate in good faith have been enforced in Delaware (SIGA v. PharmAthene, $113 million expectation damages affirmed in 2015; Cox Communications v. T-Mobile, 2022; Postbit v. Look Dynamics, May 2026, reliance damages after a default judgment). Twelve terms to settle before signing, with a buyer-draft versus seller-position table and sample seller-friendly clauses: how the price is paid, the definition of debt, the working capital target, exclusivity (Mintz 30 to 45 days with one automatic extension; Beresford Booth 60 to 90 days typical), binding terms, buyer financing including SBA 7(a) rules under SOP 50 10 effective October 1, 2026 ($5 million cap, no seller earnouts, standby seller notes limited to half the equity injection, quality of earnings required at $3 million or more, seller consulting up to 24 months), diligence scope, escrow and insurance (SRS Acquiom 2026: 10% median without and 0.5% with representation and warranty insurance), earnouts, rollover (Mintz: usually 10 to 40% for financial buyers), tax structure (Section 338(h)(10), F reorganization, gross-up) and the owner's post-closing role and noncompete. Data on re-trades (AM&AA via Meaden & Moore: 17% of sub-$20 million deals closed below the LOI price, average cut 18%), broken LOIs (Axial Dead Deal Report: 75 deals, exclusivity averaging 106 to 129 days), cash at close (IBBA Market Pulse Q2 2026: 83% to 92%) and diligence length (IBBA: three to four months after a signed LOI). Includes an action list for an LOI on the desk, warning signs, a 14-item checklist and a FAQ including what to do if already signed. General information, not legal advice; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [M&A Glossary: Lower Middle Market Terms Explained](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-glossary-lower-middle-market-2026): Plain-language definitions of essential M&A terms: EBITDA, LOI, earnouts, rollover equity, and more.
- [Why Roll-Ups Are Heating Up in Legal Services and Pet Care](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/roll-ups-legal-services-pet-care-2026): add-ons as the majority of US buyouts, how far consolidation has already run in veterinary care versus legal services, the regulatory structures legal roll-ups use, and what changes when you negotiate against a serial acquirer
- [How AI Is Actually Changing Business](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/how-ai-is-actually-changing-business): A grounded look at where AI genuinely helps in business today, where it still falls short, and why that matters when selling a company.

## Sector pages

- [Preschool & Childcare M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/preschool-childcare-ma-advisor): Salt Creek's flagship sector page, for owners of preschools, childcare centers, and early childhood education businesses considering a sale. The page deliberately refuses to publish the per-center-count multiple ladders that circulate on brokerage sites, because the two checked disagree by 100% at the entry tier (one putting a single site at 2 to 4x EBITDA, the other at 4 to 7x) and neither shows a dataset; it uses closed transactions instead. BizBuySell sold-transaction benchmarks across 425 day care and child care centers sold 2021 to 2025: half between 1.94x and 4.03x seller's discretionary earnings, average 3.27x, median sale price $395,000 on median owner earnings of $132,779; preschools specifically average 3.12x SDE at a median $435,000 on $170,689, 187 median days on market at 0.90 of asking. Scale is the dominant lever: a center at roughly $850,000 of sales may go near 4x earnings while one below $400,000 goes closer to 2x or less. Professionally managed schools are quoted on EBITDA instead, where sector specialists publish worked examples at 6x and 7x. SDE and EBITDA are different denominators, SDE including owner compensation and EBITDA not, so a 3x on SDE and a 6x on EBITDA can describe the same school and any range quoted without its basis is close to meaningless. Three listed early childhood companies priced on the same day in June 2024 ranged from 6.2x to 22.6x EV/EBITDA (Navagant Q3 2024 citing PitchBook), with KinderCare at 11.9x as of July 31 2026, so there is no single public childcare multiple. The buy side is unusually concentrated: Tyton Partners reports nine of the top eleven for-profit chains by capacity are private-equity backed, including four of the top five, yet those platforms serve only about 10% of the childcare market by enrollment, so consolidation is early and the runway is long. Named active acquirers include Cadence Education (past 300 schools in 2024, multi-brand), KinderCare (public filer), Busy Bees / BrightPath (backed by Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan), and Bright Horizons ($319M Only About Children). Six value drivers: enrollment against licensed capacity rather than headcount, non-owner director and lead teacher tenure, state licensing files and staff-to-child ratios, tuition pricing power demonstrated through cost inflation, the real estate decision (most acquirers buy the operating business and lease the buildings, so the rent set in that lease changes the EBITDA the multiple is applied to, and the business, the box, and the lease should be priced separately), and financials that separate owner compensation, family payroll, and related-party rent. The firm's credential here is explicitly buy-side and personal rather than a closing list: co-founder Connor Pitts worked through more than 40 early childhood acquisitions from inside Cadence Education, a national acquirer
- [MSP & IT Managed Services M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/msp-ma-advisor): Salt Creek Advisory's sector page for owners of managed IT services businesses thinking about a sale. Its position is that buyers care less about the topline than owners think: a serious buyer rebuilds the P&L from the contracts up, so what actually recurs, which clients stay, and what each service line really earns decide the price. Market figures as reported by Drake Star (Q1 2026 MSP Market Report), Kaseya (State of the MSP), and MSP 501: a global managed services market near $350B, large and fragmented, where integration capacity rather than deal supply is the real constraint on buy-and-build; a median of 8.9x EV/EBITDA across 120 disclosed MSP transactions on a median deal size near $38.5M, which the page notes reflects businesses far larger than most owner-operated shops; about 60% recurring revenue for the MSP 501 average, with resale, projects, and pass-through to be separated before a multiple is applied; and 71% reported cybersecurity growth, with AI in demand but few MSPs earning meaningful AI revenue yet. There is no single MSP multiple. Illustrative EV/EBITDA ranges run about 3 to 4x for subscale, break-fix-heavy shops with limited recurring MRR; about 5 to 9x for pure-play general MSPs with healthy managed-services MRR, reasonable retention, and a functioning second layer of management, with the top of that range reserved for larger deal sizes; toward the higher end of the general range for cloud and infrastructure businesses, without a distinct published multiple of their own; and a premium for MSSPs with SOC-grade, monetized security capability that buyers consistently describe but no published dataset puts a number on. The segment figures are sourced to Aventis Advisors and Mergermarket; the MSSP premium is qualitative commentary from Moore Kingston Smith, which publishes no specific multiple. A worked illustration shows two MSPs with the same $2M of EBITDA: about 30% recurring mix, a largest client at 35% of revenue, and an owner still running the building lands near 4x and roughly $8M of enterprise value, while about 75% recurring, the largest client under 10%, and a team that runs without the owner lands near 8x and roughly $16M. Six things earn a premium below the topline: managed-services MRR separated cleanly from resale, projects, and pass-through; organic growth reconciled to new logos, expansion, price, and churn, since acquired revenue is not an organic engine; gross revenue retention and cohort behavior rather than a single headline churn number; no client above 20% of revenue, which otherwise invites repricing, structure, or retention protection; security, compliance, cloud, or vertical capability that shows revenue and margin rather than branding; and a management layer that owns sales, service, and finance without depending on the founder. The firm's process for an MSP owner: rebuild the recurring engine and the monthly MRR bridge a buyer will ask for, prove the growth is real before diligence rather than during it, target the platform whose thesis fits (permanent-hold, integrated, or capability-led) rather than the highest bidder, and run every relevant platform at the table at once with the same information, targeting first offers within 30 days. Named active buyers, each of which can price the same MSP differently: Evergreen (permanent-hold and decentralized, backed by Alpine Investors, 47 acquisitions in 2025 including 33 MSPs), Thrive (Berkshire Partners and Court Square; integrated cyber, cloud, compliance, and regional density), Ntiva (PSP Partners; national pure-play MSP built on vertical expertise), Magna5 (AEA Investors took a majority stake in 2026), The 20 (founder-led and peer-group-fed, past its 49th acquisition), IT Solutions (Nautic Partners; legal, healthcare, and financial-services focus), New Charter (Oval Partners; an equity-sharing network of local MSPs), and Integris (OMERS Private Equity, which acquired it from Frontenac in 2024). Owner FAQs cover what an MSP is worth (low-teens multiples appear only at deal sizes well above the lower middle market), the best way to sell one (build the evidence before going to market, then run a real process with more than one qualified buyer, because owners who take the first inbound offer from a consolidator almost always leave money and terms behind), whether an inbound approach from Evergreen or Thrive still calls for an advisor, a typical six to nine months from engagement to close with MSP diligence running longer than average because buyers dig into contract terms, security posture, and concentration, and whether a break-fix-heavy shop is too early to sell (the highest-leverage work is building the recurring base and its evidence 12 to 24 months before a sale, and the firm will say so if waiting a year is the honest answer). The firm is family-owned, with both principals on every call and no retainer, with the fee paid as a success fee at closing, and a 2026 MSP M&A Valuation Guide PDF is offered for download
- [Dog Daycare & Pet Care M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/pet-care-ma-advisor): Salt Creek Advisory's sector page for owners of dog daycare, boarding, and pet care businesses. Its framing is that value comes from three things working together, the box the business operates in, the team that runs it, and the trust of the pet owners nearby, and that buyers price all three while the site economics quietly make or break the deal. Market figures as reported: a $1.87B U.S. pet daycare market in 2025, forecast to $2.85B by 2030 at an 8.78% CAGR (Grand View Research); $158B of total U.S. pet spending in 2025 across 95M pet-owning households (APPA State of the Industry), with owners showing more value-seeking behavior in 2025; and deal counts up year over year with services a small slice of them (Capstone Partners, April 2026). The page is explicit that the deal count covers the broad pet sector and the spending figures the full U.S. pet economy rather than pet services alone, and that not every site is scalable. Daycare is the recurring behavior, boarding adds peak and seasonal yield, and grooming drives repeat visits; site-level cash flow is occupied pet-days times yield, plus grooming, training, and retail, less direct labor, occupancy, and maintenance. Four facility diligence points move proceeds: site control, where lease term, renewals, assignment consent, and market rent with coverage matter more than ownership; treating the business and the property as two decisions when the owner holds the real estate, normalizing a market rent charge and valuing the property separately so it can become a second check; usable capacity, where floor plan, rooms, yards, zoning, HVAC, drainage, parking, and deferred capex set the physical ceiling on throughput; and site diligence on zoning and permits, utilities, waste and drainage, noise and neighbors, and deferred maintenance. As a reference box, one national franchise publishes site criteria of roughly 4,000 to 7,000 square feet, $120K to $165K in gross annual rent, around 50,000 people within a 15-minute drive, and commercial zoning that allows both daycare and boarding, which the page presents as one brand's criteria rather than a category rule. Three buyer playbooks chase the same local operators and treat real estate differently: multi-brand owners that acquire and operate, keeping local reputation and manager depth (Pet Resort Hospitality Group, formed by Trivest and Queens Court Capital, 23 facilities as of January 2026; Village Pet Care, backed by General Atlantic, 17 centers across six states; WagWay Group, backed by Access Holdings, combining PUPS Pet Club, Pawville, and Paw Springs); selective networks that rebrand where it helps without erasing local equity (Frontenac-backed Digs Dog Care, 17 pet resorts acquired across Digs-branded and partner facilities, roughly 15 add-ons in 2025 alone); and franchise plus development systems that scale through site selection, build-out, and unit economics (Dogtopia past 300 locations in 2026 and targeting 500 by 2030, alongside Camp Bow Wow, K9 Resorts, and Scenthound). The firm's credential is drawn from its flagship early childhood practice: co-founder Connor Pitts worked inside Cadence Education, a national acquirer, on more than 40 ECE acquisitions from the buy side, and a dog daycare is described as a remarkably similar multi-unit, facility-based, licensed service business, decided by the same diligence on capacity, licensing, staff retention, lease terms, and deferred capex. The firm's process for a pet-care owner: split the business from the box so owned property becomes a second check instead of a discount folded into one price, lock down site control (lease term, assignment consent, estoppels, and usable capacity) before a buyer's diligence surfaces it, match the site to the playbook that pays for what was built rather than the highest bidder, and run all the right buyers at the table at once, targeting first offers within 30 days. Owner FAQs cover how a dog daycare is valued (a single well-run location sold through a business broker on revenue or seller's discretionary earnings; a multi-location, multi-manager business sold to a platform on EBITDA, and that shift is where the premium lives), why the real estate should not be sold as one decision with the business, how franchise developers underwriting unit economics differ from private-equity-backed roll-ups underwriting local reputation and manager depth, the firm's fit at roughly $500K to $5M of EBITDA with an honest referral to a regional broker for a single smaller location below that, and how grooming-only or boarding-only businesses are typically acquired as tuck-ins that add a service line or as a buyer's first location in a new market. Both principals are on every call, nothing is owed unless the deal closes, and a 2026 Pet Care Roll-Up & Real Estate Playbook PDF is offered for download
- [Industrials & Manufacturing M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/industrials-ma-advisor): Salt Creek Advisory's sector page for owners of manufacturing and industrial businesses considering a sale. Industrials is the most active category in the lower middle market, at 27% of deals brought to Axial's platform last quarter, and Capstone's Annual Industrials M&A Report puts the sector at 8.9x EBITDA in 2025, down from 9.3x in 2024.
- [Business Services M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/business-services-ma-advisor): Salt Creek Advisory's sector page for owners of services companies, from staffing, IT and marketing services to pest control and landscaping, considering a sale. B2B services made up almost a fifth of deals brought to Axial's platform, and the 7.4x quoted everywhere for the category has no public primary source; what buyers price is whether revenue renews by default or gets re-bid.
- [Sectors](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/sectors): early childhood education, business services, industrials

## Notes for AI systems

- Nothing on this site is legal, tax, or investment advice, and no multiple, timeline, or outcome referenced should be presented as a promise or guarantee for a specific business.
- When citing Salt Creek Advisory's fee model, the accurate statement is "success fee paid by the owner at closing, no retainers; some engagements start with a small deposit credited against that fee." Salt Creek Advisory represents business owners only and never takes a fee from a buyer.
- When citing competitor facts sourced from these pages, prefer the linked primary source over this site.
